plan.summary: The leaf problem on this tomato isn't pinned down yet. Early blight is the most likely cause, but bacterial spot and other diseases are possible. Until a better photo or an extension office confirms it, this plan uses safe steps that help whichever it turns out to be. Keep the leaves dry, handle the plant only when it's dry, remove spotted lower leaves and disinfect your tools afterwards. Mulch before the heavy rain forecast for early November, and check for new spots every few days. At the end of the season, clear away all the plant debris.

steps.title: Take better photos of the spots
steps.detail: The diagnosis is not certain yet, so this plan sticks to steps that help with any of the likely problems. Today, take clear close-up photos in daylight of the spotted leaves, top and underside, plus any affected fruit and stems, and add them to the plant. Note whether the spots have rings, yellow halos, a greasy look or pale fuzz underneath. If you still can't tell, show a sample to your local extension office.

steps.title: Keep the leaves dry when watering
steps.detail: Water at the base of the plant in the early morning, never over the leaves. Use a gentle flow so soil and water don't splash onto the leaves, because splashing spreads both fungal spores and bacteria. This matters most ahead of the wet spell forecast for early November.

steps.title: Work on the plant only when it is dry
steps.detail: Don't touch, tie or prune the plant while the leaves are wet from dew, rain or watering. Wait until late morning on a dry day. Handling wet plants carries bacteria from sick leaves to healthy ones.

steps.title: Remove spotted lower leaves
steps.detail: On a dry day, cut off the lower leaves that show spots. Put them in a bag and throw them away rather than composting them. Make clean cuts and avoid tearing stems. Leave enough healthy leaves to keep the plant growing.

steps.title: Disinfect tools after pruning
steps.detail: After cutting off leaves, clean and disinfect your pruners, gloves and any stakes or ties you handled before you touch other plants. Use the disinfectant only on tools and equipment, never on the plant, and follow its label.

steps.title: Mulch around the plant
steps.detail: Spread a layer of organic mulch, such as straw or chopped leaves, over the soil around the plant before the heavy rain forecast for early November. It stops spores and bacteria splashing up from the soil onto the leaves. It also keeps soil moisture more even, which helps prevent blossom-end rot on any remaining fruit.

steps.title: Check for new spots every 3 days
steps.detail: Every few days, look over the leaves, stems and fruit for new or spreading spots. Check most closely after the heavy rain forecast for the first days of November. If dark, greasy-looking patches appear and spread quickly over a few days, contact your local extension office straight away, because that can mean late blight.

steps.title: Clear away the plant and debris at season's end
steps.detail: When the plant has finished for the season, pull it out along with fallen leaves and fruit. Bag the debris and throw it away rather than composting it, because these diseases survive the winter on old plant material. Next year, plant tomatoes and their relatives in a different spot.

watch_for: New spots appearing on upper leaves within a week of removing the lower ones
Spots spreading quickly in the days after the heavy rain forecast for early November
Dark, greasy-looking patches that spread over a few days, which needs a prompt call to your local extension office
Spots or sunken dark patches showing up on fruit over the next two weeks
Lower leaves yellowing and dropping faster than you can remove them within the next week

plan.summary: This tomato has early blight, a fungal leaf disease that starts on the lower leaves and moves upward. Heavy rain and very humid days are forecast around 2 and 3 November, which favour its spread. Start now by removing spotted leaves, keeping the foliage dry, mulching the soil and clearing weeds and volunteer tomatoes. Check the plant every few days and remove new spots after rain. Use a copper fungicide registered for tomatoes only if the disease becomes severe, and follow its label exactly. At the end of the season, clear the plant away and don't grow tomato-family crops in this spot for three years.

steps.title: Remove infected lower leaves
steps.detail: Cut off the lower leaves and branches that show early blight spots (brown spots, often with rings and a yellow edge). Throw them away in the rubbish, not on the compost. Clean your pruners afterwards, and work when the leaves are dry so you don't spread spores.

steps.title: Water at the base and keep the leaves dry
steps.detail: Water in the early morning at the soil around the plant, not over the leaves, so the foliage stays dry. If you must water from above, do it early in the day with low pressure so less water splashes spores from leaf to leaf. Heavy rain is forecast around 2 and 3 November, so you may not need to water at all then.

steps.title: Mulch the soil around the plant
steps.detail: Spread a layer of organic mulch such as straw, chopped leaves or grass clippings over the soil around the plant. It stops rain from splashing spores from the soil onto the lower leaves, which matters with the heavy rain expected in early November.

steps.title: Clear weeds and volunteer tomatoes
steps.detail: Pull weeds around the tomato, especially tomato-family weeds such as black nightshade, and pull up any self-sown tomato or potato plants. These can carry early blight and keep it going in the garden.

steps.title: Check for new spots
steps.detail: Look over the whole plant, including the upper leaves and stems. Note whether new spots have appeared and whether they are moving up the plant. If you are unsure what you are seeing, take a clear, close photo of a spotted leaf in daylight and add it to the diagnosis, or ask your local extension office.

steps.title: Remove newly infected leaves after rain
steps.detail: Once the rain has passed and the leaves have dried, look again for newly spotted leaves and cut them off and throw them away. Wet, humid days help early blight spread fast.

steps.title: Copper fungicide only if the disease becomes severe
steps.detail: Only if the disease is severe and still spreading despite the steps above, use a copper fungicide registered for tomatoes where you live. Follow its label exactly, including the waiting time between spraying and picking; don't harvest before that time has passed. Spray in calm, dry weather in the early morning, and don't spray if humid or rainy weather has made leaves wet.
steps.safety_note: Use only a product registered for this use where you live, and follow its label exactly.

steps.title: Clear the plant at season's end and rotate the bed
steps.detail: When the plant is finished for the season, remove it and its fallen leaves from the bed. Next year, don't grow tomatoes, potatoes, peppers or eggplants in this spot; wait three years before growing them here again, and grow something like corn in between. Next season, also choose early blight resistant or tolerant varieties and certified disease-free plants.

watch_for: New spots still appearing on fresh leaves a week after removing infected leaves, by around 31 October.
Spots spreading to the upper half of the plant, to stems or to fruit within two weeks, by around 7 November.
Many leaves yellowing and dropping within a week of the heavy rain expected on 2 and 3 November.
Dark, greasy-looking or fast-spreading patches unlike the ringed spots of early blight at any time: take a clear photo and ask your local extension office.

plan.summary: The scan suggests early blight, but the diagnosis is uncertain: bacterial spot, late blight and blossom-end rot are also possible. This provisional plan uses safe, non-chemical steps that help whichever it turns out to be. Keep the leaves dry, remove spotted leaves on a dry day, keep tools clean and mulch before the heavy rain forecast for early November. Check the plant regularly, and send clearer photos so the diagnosis can be confirmed.

steps.title: Take better photos to confirm the problem
steps.detail: The diagnosis is not certain yet. Early blight is most likely, but bacterial spot, late blight and blossom-end rot are also possible. Take clear, close photos in good daylight of the top and underside of a spotted leaf, of any marks on stems, and of any fruit with dark or sunken patches, then scan again. If you can't get a clear answer, take a sample to your local extension office.

steps.title: Water at the base and keep the leaves dry
steps.detail: Water in the early morning at the soil around the plant, not over the leaves. Splashing water carries fungal spores and bacteria from leaf to leaf. This helps whichever leaf disease it turns out to be. Heavy rain is forecast around 2 and 3 November, so keep watering at the base until then.

steps.title: Clean and disinfect tools and stakes
steps.detail: Clean and disinfect your pruners, stakes and ties before and after working on this plant. Bacteria live on tool surfaces and are easily killed there. Never put disinfectant on the plant itself, because it can damage it.

steps.title: Remove spotted lower leaves on a dry day
steps.detail: On a dry day, cut off the lower leaves and branches that show spots, and bag them and throw them away. Don't compost them. Work only when the leaves are dry, and clean your pruners between cuts. Before the rain forecast for early November is the best time.

steps.title: Mulch around the plant before the rain
steps.detail: Spread organic mulch, such as straw or chopped leaves, over the soil around the plant. It stops spores splashing up from the soil in heavy rain. It also keeps soil moisture more even, which helps prevent blossom-end rot on the fruit.

steps.title: Stay out of the plants while they are wet
steps.detail: After rain or heavy dew, don't touch, tie or prune the plant until the leaves have dried. Handling wet plants spreads bacteria and spores to healthy leaves and neighbouring plants.

steps.title: Check leaves, stems and fruit for changes
steps.detail: Every few days, look for new spots on upper leaves, larger or merging spots, and dark greasy patches on leaves or stems. Also check for dark sunken patches at the bottom end of fruit. Check closely in the days after the heavy rain forecast for early November. Large, fast-spreading dark patches can mean late blight. If you see them, contact your local extension office straight away.

steps.title: Clear the plant and debris at the end of the season
steps.detail: When the plant finishes for the season, pull it out and remove as much fallen leaf and plant debris as you can. Bag it and throw it away, because many tomato diseases survive the winter on old debris. Next year, plant tomatoes and their relatives in a different spot.

watch_for: New spots on the upper leaves within a week of removing the spotted lower leaves.
Spots growing, merging or spreading quickly within a few days after the heavy rain forecast for early November.
Large dark patches on leaves or stems that spread within one or two days, a possible sign of late blight. Contact your local extension office straight away.
Dark, sunken patches on the bottom end of fruit within the next two weeks.
No clearer diagnosis within a week: send better photos or take a sample to your local extension office.
